cases.task: Go straight and then turn to the right and go to the bathroom door. Go through the doorway and walk through the bathroom to the other door. You will then be in a gym. Stop when you get into this room and wait.
cases.title: Traversing Successive Rooms
cases.summary: Hybrid navigation on R2R-CE. The instruction requires passing through a bathroom to reach a gym. The observed map expands as the agent moves from the initial hallway through a bright workroom and the tiled bathroom. step and navigate_candidate requests provide complementary ways to expose and traverse the connecting doorways. The final view contains exercise equipment, and an explicit stop submits the completed task. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, Cᵢ labels candidate waypoint i, and green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example illustrates how the agent grounds an instruction whose destination is reached through several intermediate rooms. Local turning and forward movement reveal the opening beside the flower cabinet, after which a candidate request enters the bright workroom. A later view exposes the rounded wooden doorway into the bathroom, allowing the agent to continue through the tiled passage toward the exercise room. The accumulated map connects these successive observations, while the saved place descriptions associate the route with recognizable room entrances. At the endpoint, the agent's stopping summary identifies the gym through the exercise machines ahead and the bathroom behind it.

cases.task: Right now, you're facing towards the cupboard, slightly turn left and move forward. Now, slightly turn left and move forward, where you will be standing in between the couch and the sink platform. Continue to move forward until you reach an passage on the right. Now, turn right and move forward. Now, turn left and enter into the room, and stand in front of the sink and that is the end point.
cases.title: Grounding a Detailed Route in Landmarks
cases.summary: Pixel navigation and landmark recording on RxR-CE. The agent follows the passage between a couch and kitchen island, identifies the instructed right branch, and enters the room containing the sink. Pixel selections express local floor destinations, while a remember_place request records the eye-chart junction and its distinguishing geometry. The final observation shows the sink directly ahead before the task is submitted. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example shows a detailed instruction being resolved through successive local observations. The couch and white kitchen island establish the first aisle; later views reveal the hallway and the required right passage. At the junction, it records “Right passage by eye chart,” retaining the framed eye chart, narrow branch, and wooden-ceiling hallway as spatial cues. Further requests select the right passage and then the bathroom entrance in the left view. A local turn finally aligns the observation with the sink. This example illustrates landmark recording during execution; it does not require revisiting a saved place within the same task.

cases.title: From a Visible Plant to an Approach Target
cases.summary: Object grounding on HM3D v2. Starting from a living area, the agent approaches the hallway and bathroom entrance through visible free floor. Once the potted plant beside the vanity is visible, localize_object selects its image region with a bounding box. The subsequent approach ends beside the bathroom sink, where the agent submits an explicit stopping decision. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, Cᵢ labels candidate waypoint i, and green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: In this example, a category-level goal becomes a specific visual target as exploration reveals the bathroom. The first candidate request uses the stacked pictures and open hallway as local references for reaching a more informative viewpoint. From there, the agent identifies the leafy plant on the right side of the vanity and chooses another candidate through the open doorway. The bounding box in the subsequent localize_object request specifies which part of the front view should support RGB-D grounding. The recorded sequence then uses the resulting estimate for object approach. The final panorama places the plant beside the sink at close range. The example connects room-scale exploration, image-based target selection, and geometric approach, with the agent retaining responsibility for recognizing the plant and deciding when to stop.

cases.title: Turning a Landmark Description into Movement
cases.summary: Active guidance during open-vocabulary object navigation. After entering the dining area, the agent asks where to look for a decorative plant. The guide identifies a tall white pot beneath artwork beside the blue fireplace wall and describes an aisle around the dining table. A subsequent candidate request follows that aisle, and the final view shows the agent beside the indicated plant. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, Cᵢ labels candidate waypoint i, and green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example shows a question changing the information available for the next movement decision. The initial hallway observations provide an accessible route toward the living and dining area but do not yet establish a specific plant destination. The agent asks after reaching the room entrance. The answer combines appearance cues, including the white pot and artwork, with a route cue along the right side of the table. The next candidate request follows this open aisle, and later observations expose the plant beside the blue fireplace wall. In the complete record, the agent also localizes the visible plant and executes an object-approach request before stopping. The interaction thus supplies a semantic and spatial reference that can be checked against new views and acted on through the same motion interfaces used elsewhere in the framework.

cases.title: Identifying the Intended Table
cases.summary: Instance disambiguation on VL-LN. The category-level request to find a table is clarified through a description of a pale stone rectangular top on a central pedestal beneath an arched recess. The agent follows the narrow aisle, selects a point on the observed table for localization, and uses local movement to adjust its position. Its final summary refers to the same structural and spatial attributes. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, Cᵢ labels candidate waypoint i, and green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The initial view in this example contains carved wooden choir stalls, a sloped lectern, and multiple stone columns. The short task text does not specify which visible structure is the intended table, so the agent asks for distinguishing properties and a direction from its current viewpoint. The guide's answer supplies a material, shape, support structure, and architectural context. A candidate request then advances along the aisle to inspect the opening around the lectern and columns. After the pale stone table appears, a point-based localize_object request selects its flat top in the left view. The remaining recorded movements use candidate and discrete requests to approach and adjust beside it. This sequence separates target identification, geometric localization, and final positioning while preserving a consistent instance description across these decisions.

cases.title: Correcting an Ambiguous Bedroom Choice
cases.summary: Iterative clarification on CoIN. The agent first distinguishes the requested dresser from one beside a turquoise bed. A later question reveals that the furniture in a small pink-bed bedroom is also incorrect. Further guidance identifies a blue-runner passage through the kitchen. The final question verifies the long white dresser beneath a wide mirror in the larger bedroom. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, Cᵢ labels candidate waypoint i, and green markers indicate the selected waypoint or pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example illustrates how an initial interaction may be insufficient to resolve target ambiguity, requiring further clarification through subsequent questions. The guide initially describes the target as a white dresser beneath a mirror in a bedroom with a pink bedspread. However, these attributes are insufficient to distinguish between the relevant bedrooms. The agent then reaches a small bedroom with a pink bed and describes the nearby chest, mirror, chair, and TV dresser in a follow-up question. The guide explicitly rules out these candidates, prompting the agent to leave the room. The agent subsequently asks for additional route guidance. The guide identifies a passage through the kitchen near the stacked appliances and a blue runner. Following this passage, the agent eventually confirms through interaction that the intended target is the long white dresser beneath a wide mirror in the larger bedroom. This example demonstrates how active interaction and persistent memory jointly support the correction of plausible but incorrect spatial interpretations. Through successive questions, the agent progressively eliminates incorrect targets and retains the resulting corrections in memory to inform subsequent navigation decisions.

cases.task: Take the tray on the display shelves in the dining room to the wash cabinet in bathroom
cases.title: Reusing a Landmark across Ordered Subtasks
cases.summary: Continuous two-stage navigation on LHPR-VLN. The agent first reaches the dining-room tray and submits that stage with stop. It then calls navigate_place with the saved start location to return toward the initial stair landing. A pixel request selects the bathroom opening, and the recorded execution continues with candidate movements before the final stop at the wash cabinet. Both destinations are visited in one continuous sequence. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. In the panoramas, green markers indicate the selected pixel. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example illustrates two navigation stages that share the observed map and place records. In the first stage, the agent actively asks for guidance and relates the current stair-landing view to the dining-room destination using spatial cues such as the wooden aisle, white paneled wall, long table, and landscape painting. After reaching the tray, the agent records its endpoint and submits the first navigation stage. In the second stage, new guidance indicates that the bathroom lies beyond the initial stair landing, prompting the agent to explicitly return to the previously saved start location. In this way, the agent reuses familiar spatial landmarks and historical memory to guide navigation toward a new destination. Upon approaching the bathroom, the agent successfully enters the room through candidate navigation requests. The final view shows the target white vanity beneath the mirror. The two stages are submitted through separate stopping decisions and completed in the specified order within a single continuous navigation sequence.

cases.task: Follow the current GOAT-Bench subtask goal.
cases.title: Maintaining Experience across Goal Modalities
cases.summary: Selected stages of a seven-subtask GOAT-Bench sequence. The goals combine language descriptions, reference images, and an object category. The execution panels show the initial mirror search, completion of the image-specified plant subtask, and completion of the final chest subtask. The observed map retains exploration across these stages. Only subtasks 1, 2, and 7 are shown in the execution panels. Orange dots on the maps indicate the agent's position after executing the corresponding decision. Pᵢ denotes a saved place in persistent memory. Dᵢ denotes the i-th tool-level decision.
cases.analysis: The example separates changes in the goal representation from continuity of the environment. The first target is an octagonal mirror specified through relations to nearby furniture; the next is a plant specified by an image. The agent asks for the mirror's location, reaches the indicated bedroom, and records the endpoint. During the plant subtask, the recorded execution revisits start to return to the dining area where that object had been visible. Later goals extend the same map and place records. Reuse still requires checking current evidence: during the final chest search, the agent initially returns to the remembered mirror bedroom, asks whether it is the correct room, and receives a correction. It then navigates through another remembered location toward the smaller bedroom. The final frame shows the matching chest. Persistent memory thus provides reusable spatial references while interaction can correct their relevance to the current goal.

subtask_goals.text: Mirror that is octagon shaped. It is located near the dresser and the casket. Look towards the sofa chair and you will find the mirror. The mirror is also close to the tray.
Picture located on a white wall with flowers on it.
